title: What Your Generic Medicine Had To Prove — And What It Didn't
description:
Two strips. Same salt. Very different prices. Here is exactly what the cheaper one had to prove before it could be sold in India — and what it did not.

This video is about rules and published data. It is not medical advice, and nothing in it is a reason to stop taking medicine your doctor prescribed.

SOURCES
• ICH M13A, Bioequivalence for Immediate-Release Solid Oral Dosage Forms (adopted 23 July 2024)
• ICH M9, BCS-Based Biowaivers (adopted 20 November 2019)
• US FDA, Statistical Approaches to Establishing Bioequivalence
• Gazette of India, G.S.R. 327(E), 3 April 2017 — Drugs and Cosmetics (Ninth Amendment) Rules, 2017
• New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 (G.S.R. 227(E), 19 March 2019)
• Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 — CDSCO compilation, September 2024
• CDSCO, Guidelines for Bioavailability & Bioequivalence Studies, March 2005
• Davit et al., Annals of Pharmacotherapy, 2009;43(10):1583–97

beats.text: Two strips of tablets. [[0.8]] Same salt. Same strength. Same number of tablets. One costs a fraction of what the other costs. And the person holding both of them asks the chemist the same question that gets asked in every medical shop in this country, every single day. [[1.0]] Is it the same? [[1.2]] The honest answer is not yes. [[0.6]] And it is not no.

The honest answer is that there is a specific thing the cheaper strip had to prove before it was allowed to be sold. [[0.9]] There is a number attached to it. And in India, that requirement applies to two of the four categories that medicines are sorted into. [[1.4]] Not all four. None of that is hidden. It is written in a gazette notification from April two thousand and seventeen that anyone can download. [[0.8]] Almost nobody has read it. Today we are going to read it.

Start with the thing most people get wrong. When a company makes a generic version of a medicine, it is not copying a recipe. [[0.7]] It does not get the original manufacturer's formula. It does not get their machines, their suppliers, or their tablet press. It gets one thing: the name of the active molecule.

Everything else, the generic manufacturer works out on its own. The binder that holds the tablet together. The coating. The filler that makes up most of the tablet's weight. The compression force. The particle size of the drug itself. [[1.0]] So the tablet is genuinely a different object. Same molecule inside. Different everything else. And that matters, because the molecule does not do anything while it is still a tablet. [[0.8]] It has to dissolve. It has to cross the wall of your intestine. It has to reach your blood.

A tablet that dissolves too slowly delivers less drug. [[0.5]] One that dissolves too fast can deliver a sharper peak than intended. So the question regulators actually ask is not, is it the same tablet. [[0.9]] It is: does the same amount of drug reach the blood, at the same speed? That question has a name. Bioequivalence.

To answer it, you need to measure two things in actual human beings. The first is how much drug gets into the blood in total. On a graph of drug concentration against time, that is the area underneath the curve. In the literature it is written as A U C. The second is how high the concentration peaks, and that is written as C max. [[0.6]] A U C tells you the total dose that arrived. Cmax tells you how hard it hit.

rows.label: AUC  —  total drug that reached the blood

beats.text: Now, how do you compare two products on those numbers without the comparison being ruined by the fact that people are different from each other? [[0.8]] You use the same people for both. A bioequivalence study is usually a crossover. [[0.7]] A volunteer takes the generic. You draw blood at intervals and plot the curve. Then, after a gap long enough for the drug to clear completely, the same volunteer takes the original product, and you plot that curve too. Same body. Same liver. Same gut. [[0.9]] The only thing that changed is the tablet.

Here is the standard, and it is the same sentence in Washington, in Amsterdam, at the World Health Organization, and in C D S C O's own guidance in Delhi. [[0.9]] The ninety percent confidence interval for the ratio of the two products, on both A U C and Cmax, must fall between eighty point zero zero percent and one hundred twenty five point zero zero percent.

card.caption: The whole confidence interval must fit inside
card.source: ICH M13A  ·  US FDA  ·  EMA  ·  WHO  ·  CDSCO 2005 guidance

beats.text: Now. [[1.0]] Almost everybody who hears that number for the first time hears it as: so a generic can be twenty percent weaker, or twenty five percent stronger. [[1.2]] That reading is wrong, and it is worth understanding exactly why, because this single misunderstanding is the source of most of the distrust. Two reasons.

The first is that eighty and one hundred twenty five are not two different sized allowances. [[0.7]] They are the same allowance. The calculation is done on logarithms, and on that scale the two limits sit at exactly the same distance from one hundred, in opposite directions. The lopsided look of twenty and twenty five is an artefact of converting back to ordinary percentages at the end. Nothing about the rule is lopsided.

The second reason matters more. [[1.0]] The rule does not say the result must land between eighty and one hundred twenty five. It says the entire confidence interval must fit inside that range. A confidence interval is a measure of how unsure you are. [[0.6]] A sloppy study with few volunteers and noisy data produces a wide interval, and a wide interval will not fit. [[0.8]] To squeeze the whole interval inside those limits, your result has to sit close to one hundred, and your study has to be good enough to prove it. [[1.0]] A product that really delivered twenty percent less drug would produce an interval reaching well below eighty. [[0.7]] It would fail.

That is the theory. [[0.8]] Theory is not evidence. What actually happens? The United States Food and Drug Administration answered this about its own approvals. Researchers from the agency's generic drugs office reviewed two thousand and seventy bioequivalence studies for oral generic products approved over twelve years, from nineteen ninety six to two thousand and seven. [[1.0]] Here is what they found.

rows.label: Approved in the United States — not India

beats.text: The average difference between the generic and the original, on total drug absorbed, was three point five six percent. On peak concentration, four point three five percent. [[0.9]] And the spread: for total absorption, ninety seven point six percent of those studies came in under a ten percent difference. [[0.7]] Just over two percent exceeded ten percent. So the rule permits a window. [[0.6]] In practice, products land nowhere near its edges. [[1.4]] Now the part that most people quoting this study leave out. That is American data. [[0.8]] It tells you what the science can do. [[0.9]] It does not tell you what happened to the strip in your hand.

To know what happened to the strip in your hand, you have to follow how a medicine gets licensed in this country. [[0.8]] And India has two gates, not one. The first gate is central. Under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules of two thousand and nineteen, a drug is legally a new drug for four years from the date the central authority first permitted it. [[0.7]] Some categories are new forever. Modified release formulations. Novel delivery systems. Vaccines. Products made from living cells.

While a drug is still a new drug, anyone who wants to make their own version applies centrally, to the Drugs Controller General of India. [[0.9]] And the schedule of data they must submit includes, in plain words, bioavailability or bioequivalence studies for oral dosage forms. So within those first four years, the answer is clean. [[0.6]] A generic of an oral medicine had to prove bioequivalence, and a central authority reviewed the proof. [[1.3]] Then the four years end. [[0.9]] And the file moves.

After four years, a company wanting to manufacture that same molecule does not go to Delhi. [[0.7]] It applies to the licensing authority of its own state. Around thirty six state and union territory authorities. [[0.6]] Different offices, different capacity, same rulebook. And here is the part worth sitting with. [[1.0]] Before April two thousand and seventeen, at that second gate, there was no bioequivalence requirement at all. Not a weak one. [[0.7]] Not a loophole. Simply no clause requiring it.

items.headline: Before April 2017: no bioequivalence clause at the state gate
Applies to oral dosage forms in BCS category II and IV

beats.text: That changed on the third of April, two thousand and seventeen, with a gazette notification numbered G S R three two seven E. It did two things. [[0.8]] It wrote a definition into the rules, of something called the Biopharmaceutics Classification System. And it added one sentence, identically, into five different rules covering every kind of state manufacturing licence. The sentence says the applicant shall submit the result of a bioequivalence study along with the application, for oral dosage forms of drugs in category two and category four of that classification system. [[1.4]] Category two. And category four. There are four categories.

Before anyone decides this is a scandal, understand why those two categories were chosen. [[0.8]] Because the choice is not arbitrary, and it is not lazy. It is the single most defensible line they could have drawn. The classification sorts drug molecules on two properties. Solubility: will the full dose dissolve in a glass of water's worth of fluid, across the range of acidity your gut actually has? [[0.6]] And permeability: once dissolved, does it cross the intestinal wall easily?

rows.label: Category I  —  dissolves well, absorbs well
Category III  —  dissolves well, absorbs poorly

beats.text: Two properties, high or low, gives four categories. [[0.9]] Category one is high and high. Category two is poorly soluble. Category three is poorly permeable. Category four is poor at both. Now, the logic. [[1.0]] If a drug dissolves completely and almost instantly, and crosses the gut wall easily, then the tablet around it stops mattering. [[0.7]] It has already released everything it had before absorption begins. You can show that with a dissolution test in a laboratory, and you do not need volunteers. Internationally that shortcut has a name, a biowaiver, and it is available to categories one and three.

Categories two and four cannot have it. [[0.8]] When a drug dissolves poorly, how fast it dissolves is the thing that decides how much gets absorbed. And how fast it dissolves depends on the formulation. [[0.6]] Particle size. Coating. Excipients. For those drugs, a different tablet really can mean a different dose reaching the blood. [[1.2]] So the two thousand and seventeen rule targets exactly the drugs where formulation matters most, and exempts exactly the ones where it provably does not. [[0.8]] Whoever drafted it understood the pharmacology.

So where does that leave the strip in your hand? [[1.0]] If the molecule is still inside its four year window, or is a modified release form, a bioequivalence study was required and centrally reviewed. If it is past four years and falls in category two or four, a study was required, submitted to a state licensing authority. [[1.2]] And if it is past four years and falls in category one or three, there is no statutory bioequivalence requirement. [[0.8]] Dissolution testing, yes. A study in human volunteers, no.

Now, that is defensible. [[0.7]] The science says those are the drugs where the tablet matters least. But notice what the international version of that shortcut requires. [[0.9]] Under the international guideline, a biowaiver is not automatic for being in category one. You must show the product dissolves at least eighty five percent within fifteen to thirty minutes, at three different acidity levels, and for category three the excipients must closely match the original. [[1.0]] It is a test you have to pass. Not a category you get to belong to. And the Indian rules do not say who decides which category a drug sits in. [[0.8]] There is no published national list attached to the clause.

There is one more thing, and it is the honest end of this story. [[0.9]] Remember the American study. Two thousand and seventy products, average difference under four percent. That number exists because a regulator reviewed its own decisions and published the result. [[1.3]] There is no Indian equivalent. [[0.8]] Not a hidden one. Not a classified one. As far as a careful search of the published literature can establish, it has not been done, or it has not been released.

card.caption: Categories that need a bioequivalence study in India
card.source: G.S.R. 327(E), 3 April 2017 · as in CDSCO's compilation of the Rules, Sept 2024

beats.text: So the honest position is this. [[0.7]] The rule is scientifically well aimed. The gap in it is real, documented, and narrower than it first looks. [[0.9]] And the study that would tell us whether the gap matters in practice has not been published. [[1.4]] Which brings me to the only thing I want you to take from this. Nothing here is a reason to stop taking your medicine. [[0.9]] An untreated condition is a certain harm. A theoretical difference in absorption, in a category chosen because formulation barely affects it, is not. [[0.7]] If anything in this video worries you about something you take, the person to ask is your doctor or your pharmacist, not a comment section.

What this is, is an answer to the question at the counter. [[1.0]] Not, yes it is the same. Not, no it is not. [[0.8]] It is: here is exactly what it had to prove. [[0.6]] Here is what it did not. [[1.0]] And here is the document where both of those are written down. [[1.2]] The paperwork told you first. [[0.8]] It usually does.
